idiom_name: hand-rolled symantic as a struct of function pointers over void* carriers
implementation_notes: C can host the final encoding only in its weakened, untyped form: the algebra becomes a struct of function pointers, the interpretation type collapses to void* (or to one fixed concrete type), and each interpreter is another instance of that struct; a program is a function taking the struct. What the pattern actually needs - a host type checker that can see the interpretation type and prove the interpreters total - is exactly what void* erases, so the encoding degrades into an unchecked convention where any interpreter may return the wrong shape and no operation is checked at compile time. Use it only when a single monomorphic algebra is interpreted into one fixed carrier type and the function-pointer table buys something over a switch.
pitfalls: void* erases the interpreted type: an interpreter that returns the wrong shape is a runtime fault, not a compile error - the property the pattern exists for is gone.
Function-pointer tables cannot be resolved implicitly, so every call site threads the symantic struct by hand; forgetting to pass the intended interpreter silently uses another meaning.
A monomorphic carrier forces one DSL type; the moment the DSL needs two result types the table has to return a tagged union, i.e. the initial encoding the pattern was meant to avoid.
alternative: Keep the DSL as data - a tagged union struct plus a dispatch function per interpretation - and make the interpreter injectable, or generate one specialised interpreter per target with the preprocessor/code generation; reserve function-pointer tables for single-carrier algebras.
